The common two-banded sea bream, Diplodus vulgaris, is a demersal sparid widely distributed along the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic coasts. Field surveys indicate that adults typically attain a maximum recorded total length of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], a value that places this species among the medium-sized members of its genus. Sexual maturation in this species is characteristically tied to body size, with the onset of gonadal recrudescence occurring once individuals surpass a total length of 17 cm [Lp = 17 cm]. This threshold marks a significant physiological transition from the juvenile stage to the reproductively viable adult phase. In the laboratory, newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion following an incubation period of just 4 days [ab = 4 days] when maintained at a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This rapid eclosion, which releases a prolarva still heavily dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves, is comparable to the developmental rates documented in congeneric species such as Diplodus puntazzo and reflects the accelerated embryogenesis typical of summer-spawning sparids in warm coastal waters.

Reproductive output in Diplodus vulgaris has been assessed through both field observations and controlled aquarium studies. Under stable thermal conditions at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], a temperature that approximates the peak spawning season in the central Mediterranean, females have been observed to produce approximately 536,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 536,000 eggs per spawning event], with a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year]. This high fecundity per event is characteristic of an iteroparous batch spawner that releases multiple egg batches over an extended reproductive season. The eggs themselves are small and pelagic, and the wet weight of an individual fertilised ovum, estimated from the egg diameter of 0.85 mm recorded in the related sparid Diplodus sargus, is approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams]. This minimal initial mass underscores the yolk-dependent, lecithotrophic strategy of the early prolarva, which must rapidly develop functional feeding apparatus before its endogenous reserves are exhausted.

The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult of this species is approximately 1,500 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,500 grams], a mass that is typically reached only after several years of sustained somatic growth in productive coastal habitats. This asymptotic body mass is consistent with the maximum total length of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm] and reflects the typical allometric scaling relationships observed within the Sparidae. The 1,500 gram [Wwi = 1,500 gram] adult represents the culmination of a growth trajectory that begins with the near-microscopic 0.00032 gram [Wwb = 0.00032 gram] hatchling, involving a mass increase spanning several orders of magnitude. This extreme disparity between neonatal and adult mass underscores the importance of the planktonic larval and demersal juvenile stages as periods of rapid mass accumulation, during which the fish must efficiently convert ingested prey into somatic tissue to reach the size necessary for successful benthic settlement and eventual reproduction.

Longevity in Diplodus vulgaris, based on otolith-based age estimates from wild populations, suggests a maximum lifespan of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This lifespan, which is broadly consistent with the values reported for other temperate sparids of comparable body size, was recorded from individuals inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature near 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. Because the onset of sexual maturity is tied to the attainment of a total length of 17 cm [Lp = 17 cm], a size that is usually achieved within the first two to three years of life, the species enjoys a relatively long reproductive window as an iteroparous adult. The combination of a moderate lifespan, a body size ceiling of 45 cm [Li = 45 cm], and an adult mass of 1,500 grams [Wwi = 1,500 grams] positions D. vulgaris as a typical example of a slow-to-medium life history pace within its guild of coastal rocky-bottom sparids.

The early life stages of Diplodus vulgaris are particularly sensitive to thermal conditions, which can dramatically influence developmental scheduling and survival rates. In controlled experiments conducted at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the yolk-sac larva transitions from an endotrophic, lecithotrophic existence to the onset of exogenous feeding very rapidly after the eclosion that occurs at 4 days [ab = 4 days]. The first feeding larva must begin capturing planktonic prey almost immediately upon mouth opening to avoid the point of no return associated with irreversible starvation. Within the broader context of the species’ life history, the rapid age at birth of 4 days [ab = 4 days] contrasts sharply with the maximum longevity of 10 years [am = 10 years], highlighting the extreme selection pressure on early survival versus the extended adult reproductive phase at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The maintenance of such a high daily reproductive output of approximately 1,469 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 1,469 eggs per day] at the spawning temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] is an adaptive response to the exceptionally high mortality rates experienced during the pelagic larval phase.
